answer: Two problem statements: a word dictionary without any database, and a superfast key-value store (both used in production; chosen to build foundational blocks).
evidence: Overview: 'The agenda is two problem statements: a word dictionary without any database, and a superfast key-value store.'

answer: Ruled out: every traditional/off-the-shelf database - MySQL, Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, Memcache, nothing. Relaxed: performance - a high response time is acceptable (caching/batching etc. are known ways to speed up). Demanded: portability - literally one portable file.
evidence: Ch1 §1.1: 'no MySQL, no Postgres, no MongoDB, no Redis, no Elasticsearch, no Memcache, nothing'; 'Performance is not today's problem. A high response time is acceptable'; 'What is required is portability.'

answer: No live, pointed updates. Once a week (say every Sunday) the publisher sends a changelog file by email holding only the words that changed and their new meanings; you apply it to the store. One huge processing pass a week is acceptable.
evidence: Ch1 §1.1: 'Once a week, say every Sunday, a changelog file arrives by email holding only the words that changed and their new meanings, and you apply it to whatever store you have built.'

answer: A lookup is always a single word: given a word return its meaning, else 404; no autocomplete. It is a key-value store (word -> two/three-line meaning). Size: 1 TB total, 170,000 words (deliberately big, several MB per word, e.g. imagine multimedia).
evidence: Ch1 §1.1: 'A lookup is always a single word. There is no autocomplete... if the word does not exist, return 404. The whole dictionary is 1 TB, and it holds 170,000 words.'

answer: Storage, query, portability and seamless updates.
evidence: Ch1 §1.1: 'Every design that follows is judged on four axes: storage, query, portability and seamless updates.'

answer: To check whether one word exists you must read the entire JSON file, deserialize/unmarshal it (very expensive) and build an in-memory object such as a hash map before checking; at 1 TB that is really costly and the format gives no direct way to reach one entry. (JSON Lines streams but still has no index, so still a scan.)
evidence: Ch1 §1.2: 'to check whether one word exists, you read the entire JSON file, deserialize it, build an in-memory object such as a hash map, and only then check.'

answer: A plain CSV-like text file, one line per word: the word, a comma, its meaning, newline (e.g. 'apple,a fruit', then 'amazon,a rainforest'...). A write-ahead-log style format was suggested but not taken up.
evidence: Ch1 §1.2: 'It is CSV-like, one line per word: apple,a fruit, a newline, then amazon and its meaning'; Fig 1·b.

answer: The dictionary must not contain the same word twice (no repetitive entries) - so an update can't simply be written as another line. Why: there are no columns, only words and meanings; imagine the file opened in a text editor with repeats in it; a portable file can't carry duplicates.
evidence: Ch1 §1.2: 'the dictionary must not contain the same word twice... imagine the file opened in any text editor with repeats in it, and remember that a portable file can't carry duplicates.'

answer: No - response time isn't a constraint, so sorting brings nothing yet; words can sit in any order. Accepted for starters (it comes back in 5.3 for the weekly update).
evidence: Ch1 §1.2: 'The first answer was no: response time isn't a constraint, so sorting brings nothing yet... For starters, that is accepted.'

answer: Very read-heavy: a thousand reads to one write would understate it; the real ratio is much more skewed (much greater than 1000:1).
evidence: Ch1 §1.1: 'a thousand reads to one write would understate it, and the real ratio is much more skewed than that'; card 'read-heavy: ≫ 1000 : 1'.

answer: A single-word update indeed cannot be very costly (shouldn't 'boil the ocean' with heavy IO or scanning every file), but since updates arrive as one weekly batch, one huge processing pass a week is acceptable.
evidence: Ch1 §1.1: 'A single-word update indeed cannot be very costly. But updates arrive as one weekly batch, so one huge processing pass a week is acceptable.'

answer: It kills portability: with multiple files the dictionary is no longer one file. A single zip of many folders was also rejected: you'd still have to extract it to use it; it is still many logical files, often compressed, so no direct byte-offset read into the data.
evidence: Ch1 §1.3: 'Rejected: with multiple files you kill portability'; zip: 'you would still have to extract it to use it. It is still many logical files, often compressed, so there is no direct byte-offset read'.

answer: AWS Athena: upload a plain CSV to S3 and query it seamlessly (in the lecture's telling, Athena keeps an index handy with the file; the page notes Athena actually scans files, not a per-key index). Parquet/Avro set aside because not many people know these formats and the aim is to keep it really simple; Lucene's good parts kept one level down - simple version first, then the next level.
evidence: Ch1 §1.3 'What this simulates': Athena; Parquet 'Not today. Not many people know these formats, and the aim is to keep it really simple'; Lucene 'Good parts, kept one level down for now'.

answer: All that (binary search, B+ tree pages, 8 KB blocks, 1,000 keys in memory) is over-engineering for a very simple word dictionary; and why only 1,000 keys in memory - far more fit. No B+ trees, nothing fancy; keep it very simple, that's where you see the power and beauty of the system. (Only the offset idea survives.)
evidence: Ch2 §2.1: 'And why only 1,000 keys in memory? Far more fit. For a very simple word dictionary all of this is over-engineering: no B+ trees, nothing fancy.'

answer: Open the file, read line by line until the key is found, stop, read the meaning and return it. Worst case reads the whole 1 TB per request; on average half, 0.5 TB = 500 GB per request, and every request pays it again.
evidence: Ch2 §2.1: 'In the worst case every request reads the whole 1 TB file; on average it reads half of it, 0.5 TB, which is 500 GB per request.'

answer: It degrades the disk's performance and wears the disk out - sectors go bad from heavy overuse. A hardware problem, a software problem and a time problem at once.
evidence: Ch2 §2.1: 'degrades the disk's performance, and wears the disk out: its sectors go bad... a hardware problem, a software problem and a time problem at once.'

answer: Indexing (and then do the number crunch: how big will the index be, does it fit in memory?).
evidence: Ch2 §2.1 rule: 'Whenever reads are slow, the only thing that should come to your mind is indexing.'

answer: Each entry holds the key (word) and its offset in the data file. The offset is the byte position where the word's line starts - the nth byte from the start of the file, a count of bytes, not a line number (e.g. apple at 0, amazon at 14, book at 34).
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'Each index entry holds two things: the key and its offset... It is a count of bytes, not a line number.'

answer: The data scan wades through every huge meaning; the index holds only keys and small offsets, so you're not iterating over megabytes of meanings, and the small index file is very fast to read sequentially even in the worst case (a couple of MB vs a terabyte).
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'The index holds only keys and small offsets... so you are not iterating over megabytes of meanings, and the small index file is very fast to read sequentially, even in the worst case.'

answer: You'd still have to go through every word under that letter to find the one you want, while a per-word offset takes you straight to its line; and the full per-word index fits in memory anyway, so splitting by letter buys nothing.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'you would still have to go through every word under that letter... the full per-word index fits in memory anyway'.

answer: Entry size = length of key + length of offset + 2: average English word ~4.3 characters (instructor computed it; not more than five) + 4-byte integer offset + 1 comma + 1 newline = 10.3 bytes. (Page notes: a 1 TB file needs 8-byte offsets -> 14.3 B; distinct-word average ~7.6.)
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'So an entry is about 4.3 + 4 + 2 = 10.3 bytes.'

answer: 170,000 x 10.3 B = 1,751,000 B, about 1.751 MB (about 2.4 MB with 8-byte offsets). It fits in RAM easily - 'peanuts' beside 1 TB - so load it into an in-memory hash map at server start, and every lookup becomes one pointed read.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: '170,000 × 10.3 B = 1,751,000 B... about 1.75 MB'; 'An index of 1.75 MB fits in RAM very easily. Next to a 1 TB data file it is peanuts.'

answer: Number crunching matters when designing any system: what looked huge (1 TB, 170,000 words) needs an index of under two megabytes; the number crunch, not a cleverer structure, settled the design. Also don't take megabytes lightly.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'This is why number crunching matters when you design any system. What looked huge... needs an index of under two megabytes.'

answer: Index stored on disk; at API server start, load it into an in-memory hash map. A request checks the map for the word, gets the offset, goes to the data file, reads the line at that offset and returns the meaning.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'A request checks the map for the word, gets the offset, goes to the data file, reads the line at that offset and returns the meaning.'

answer: index.dict (couple of MB of words and offsets) and data.dict (the TB of meanings). Two files break portability: anyone copying the dictionary must copy both and keep them together, whereas the brief said literally one file.
evidence: Ch3 §3.1: 'Two files, an index and a data.dictionary, break portability. Anyone who copies the dictionary has to copy both and keep them together'.

answer: Every startup would then iterate through the entire terabyte of data just to rebuild something that hasn't changed; the file changes only once a week, so the work is avoidable. Store the index.
evidence: Ch3 §3.1: 'every startup then iterates through the entire terabyte of data just to rebuild something that hasn't changed. The file changes once a week, so the work is avoidable.'

answer: How does the reader know where the index ends and the data begins? (Otherwise it reads data lines into the map as index entries.) First two options: a special separator line/marker between index and data, and a pre-allocated fixed-size region (first 2 MB is the index).
evidence: Ch3 §3.1 Fig 3·a: 'where does the index stop?' '– special line / separator · – pre-allocate / fixed size · 2 MB'.

answer: 'A very nice hack': the reader knows the first 2 MB are index without searching (a bit more than 1.751 MB since few words are added weekly), but it wastes a little space, and the push was to be more frugal.
evidence: Ch3 §3.1: 'A very nice hack, in the lecture's words, though it wastes a little space, and the push was to be more frugal.'

answer: It still leaves the original problem: on the day the two meet, how do you know where one finished and the other begins? The gap between them is unused space until then, and the fallback was again a separator.
evidence: Ch3 §3.1: 'on the day the two meet, how do you know where one finished and the other begins? The gap between them is unused space... the fallback, once more, was a separator.'

answer: Store the byte offset (the boundary - finally the index size) directly as a number at the start of the file instead of a separator, so nothing is searched for. The general name: a (fixed-size) file header - the classic mechanism of file formats (PNG, JPG, MP3, AVI).
evidence: Ch3 §3.2: 'store the byte offset directly at the start of the file... That first chunk is a header, and it is the classic mechanism of file formats everywhere'.

answer: 1) magic name 'OUR_DICT' - 8 bytes; 2) version - 4 bytes; 3) index size - 4 bytes. Total 16 bytes, fixed size.
evidence: Ch3 §3.2: 'a fixed-width header of 16 bytes: 8 for the name, 4 for the version, 4 for the index size.'

answer: Magic name tells the decoder 'this is our dictionary' (like PNG's first bytes saying PNG; the instructor's own DB would start with AODB). Version: one format can have variants, e.g. v1 index first then data, v2 data first then index; the decoder reads the version and acts accordingly (it describes the format/layout, not the data).
evidence: Ch3 §3.2: 'a name that tells the decoder this is our dictionary'; 'Version 1 might store the index first and then the data; version 2 the data first and then the index.'

answer: 1) Read the first 16 bytes as the header. 2) First 8 say OUR_DICT - our dictionary. 3) Next 4 give the version; the decoder acts on it. 4) Next 4 give the index size (e.g. 1,751,000); read exactly that many bytes as the index. 5) Build the in-memory hash map from the index (apple->0, amazon->14...). 6) Everything after is data, which the offsets point into; server ready.
evidence: Ch3 §3.2 Fig 3·c 'Opening the file' steps 1–6.

answer: Other formats are also built from sections with a header: in an MP4 the header says where the video part and the audio part are, video holding its frames and audio its waveform info (JPG has its frames). (Page notes MP4 muxers usually write the moov index at the end, with faststart to move it to the front.)
evidence: Ch3 §3.3: 'in an MP4, the header says where the video part is and where the audio part is'; §3.2 note on moov.

answer: JSON has no header: it's a simple text file, so to get anything out you read the whole file and let the decoder parse braces/quotes/strings into an in-memory dictionary. Parquet has header/metadata information (strictly a footer: PAR1, column chunks, file metadata + 4-byte length, PAR1); a reader reads the footer first to find just the column chunks it needs.
evidence: Ch3 §3.3: 'JSON has no header... you read the entire file'; 'Parquet... also has headers and information. Strictly, Parquet keeps that information in a footer... a reader reads the footer first to find the column chunks it needs'.

answer: Encoder creates a file in that format; decoder decodes/reads it (images, video, audio, any format). 'This browser does not support TIF' means the browser has no decoder for TIFF: given those bytes, it doesn't know how to interpret them.
evidence: Ch3 §3.3: 'The encoder creates a file in that specific format; the decoder decodes it'; 'It means the browser has no decoder for that format'.

answer: [Header 16 B: OUR_DICT (8 B) | version (4 B) | index size (4 B)] | index (word,offset entries, index_size bytes) | data (word,meaning entries; offsets point here).
evidence: Ch3 §3.2 struct dict_header and Fig 3·b: 'OUR_DICT · ver · size · index… · data…'.

answer: End user -> load balancer -> one of a bunch of API servers, which expose GET /word returning the word's meaning (servers read the dictionary from storage).
evidence: Ch4 §4.1: 'A request from the end user comes to a load balancer, and behind the load balancer sits a bunch of API servers... a GET on /word'.

answer: 1) Updates become tedious (every server updated, some may be unavailable) - fine, weekly bulk job. 2) Inconsistency if an update partially fails - fine, meanings barely change. 3) Cost: same 1 TB file duplicated on every server (100 servers = 100 TB redundant, typically on costly SSDs). Cost is the biggest pain.
evidence: Ch4 §4.1: 'The biggest pain is cost: the same file stored again and again... Tedious updates and brief inconsistency you can live with'.

answer: Real-world design is doing the bare minimum things at the bare minimum cost; if you're not thinking about cost you're not building good systems - cost-efficiency first, before speed. You can make anything faster by throwing money at a cloud provider: 1 TB RAM per machine to hold the whole dictionary in one hash table, no index - fast but not a good solution because not cost-effective.
evidence: Ch4 §4.1 rule and: 'Put one terabyte of RAM on each machine... It would be fast, and it would not be a good solution, because it is not cost effective.'

answer: Because replicating to every server is cost-inefficient, and what is common across multiple servers is the network - so the dictionary needs a common place accessible over the network.
evidence: Ch4 §4.2: 'what is common across multiple servers? The network. So the dictionary needs a common place that is accessible over the network.'

answer: S3's get-object call takes parameters for the bytes you want to read (a byte range), so you can fetch just the header and index bytes, then just the byte range at a word's offset (HTTP Range header, 206 Partial Content).
evidence: Ch4 §4.2: 'S3's get-object call takes parameters for the bytes you want to read.'

answer: Random reads: from this file, at this offset, read n bytes - written as (file, offset, n) / (file, off, n), like seeking on a normal disk.
evidence: Ch4 §4.2: 'one feature is required: random reads... (file, offset, n)'; Fig 4·b '(file, off, n)'.

answer: Any network attached storage with file-system semantics/random reads: HDFS, literal physical network hard disks in a data center (Dell's), a NAS share. S3 was used only because everyone understands it (also very cheap, optimized for blob storage).
evidence: Ch4 §4.2: 'Any network attached storage with the same semantics would do: HDFS, or literal physical network hard disks... S3 is used only because everyone understands it.'

answer: Only the dictionary's file path on S3 (static config for now). At boot: one S3 (ranged) read of the first 16 bytes as the header (is it our dictionary, index size), then a second S3 call reading exactly index-size bytes of index, build the in-memory hash table, then serve. Two calls at boot.
evidence: Ch4 §4.3: 'Only the dictionary's file path on S3... read the first 16 bytes... Make another S3 call to read that many bytes of index'.

answer: Any API server checks its in-memory hash table: word missing -> 404 without touching S3; present -> take the offset and do one random/ranged read on the S3 file at that offset for that many bytes, return the meaning (200).
evidence: Ch4 §4.3: 'If the word isn't there, return 404. If it is, take the offset and do a random read on the S3 file at that offset, for that many bytes.'

answer: Being able to fire pointed queries at S3 and read a single record without reading the entire file - only the bytes of interest - effectively building a database (key-value store) on S3.
evidence: Ch4 §4.3: 'Being able to fire pointed queries at S3 without reading the whole file was called magical'.

answer: On a separate machine (a newly spun-up server), not the API servers - a periodic (cron-like) job. It starts with the changelog and downloads the current dictionary from S3.
evidence: Ch5 §5.1: 'the update job runs on a newly spun-up server. That server holds the changelog, and it downloads the current dictionary from S3.'

answer: The dictionary would keep growing forever and would hold duplicate entries, and the served dictionary can't have repeated entries.
evidence: Ch5 §5.1: 'Then the dictionary keeps growing forever, and it holds duplicate entries, and the dictionary being served can't have repeated entries.'

answer: Because the changelog already states exactly what has to change. It's easy to build complex systems and very hard to build simple ones; think only about what you really need.
evidence: Ch5 §5.1: 'Neither is needed, because the changelog already states exactly what has to change.'

answer: The bytes are written blindly over what's there: the 20-byte 'apple,a round fruit' line is 6 bytes longer than the 14-byte old line, so its last six bytes land on bytes 14-19, overwriting 'ball,a'; ball doesn't move down and the word ball is lost (file reads 'apple,a round fruit' then 'round object'). Editors shift lines only because text is in memory.
evidence: Ch5 §5.2 Fig 5·b steps 3–4: 'its last six bytes, fruit⏎, land on bytes 14–19... The word ball is lost.'

answer: Product manager, architect and engineer. The engineer hat - thinking through the code you would actually write - exposes it.
evidence: Ch5 §5.2: 'always wears three hats: product manager, architect and engineer. Thinking through the code is what the engineer hat looks like.'

answer: The served dictionary must not contain repeated entries, and for a weekly batch update you should simply build the clean file directly; graveyards belong with live updates (it returns for the second engine, 8.3).
evidence: Ch5 §5.2: 'The served dictionary must not contain repeated entries, and for a weekly batch update, you should simply build the clean file directly. Graveyards belong with live updates'.

answer: Write a new file: walk the words, write changes in their place into a new file, the rest of the old file after - not naive, the best approach here. It is the merge step of merge sort (merge two sorted lists into a third).
evidence: Ch5 §5.3: 'It isn't naive. It is the merge step of merge sort, and given this design it is the best approach.'

answer: The dictionary file must be sorted (both inputs sorted). The changelog is very short: if not sorted, load it in memory, sort it and write it back out.
evidence: Ch5 §5.3: 'the dictionary file needs to be sorted'; 'If it isn't sorted, load it in memory, sort it and write it back out; it is small enough.'

answer: a-a', b-b', c-c'', d-d', e-e', f-f'', g-g', h-h' (8 lines; c and f take the changelog meanings, e is new).

answer: The job server's disk must hold at least 2 TB (old 1 TB dictionary plus the ~1 TB merged file); acceptable since it's just one server.
evidence: Ch5 §5.3: 'the disk of the server spun up for the job must hold at least two terabytes. That's acceptable: it is just one server.'

answer: While the file uploads there may be a short window when it can't be served; and any deployment needs a rollback plan - if the upload fails or the file is corrupted, monitoring must catch it and revert to the previous file. evidence: Ch6 §6.1: 'Two objections came up. While the file uploads there may be a short window when it can't be served. And any deployment needs a rollback plan'.

answer: A server's in-memory index says apple is at byte offset 100, 1,024 bytes long. After the new file lands at the same path, a query for apple still reads 1,024 bytes from offset 100, but in the new file those bytes may be another word (e.g. the one before apple), possibly starting mid-line; apple's real offset differs, so the user sees garbage until every server reloads its index.
evidence: Ch6 §6.1: 'a query for apple still goes to offset 100 and reads 1,024 bytes. In the new file those bytes may be some other word... the user sees garbage.'

answer: What if the upload fails? What if the file is corrupted? And API servers must be told to reload their index immediately (for that whole duration users see garbage - very poor UX). Also no copy to roll back to (unless versioning). A periodic refresh doesn't fix it.
evidence: Ch6 §6.1: 'Uploading to the same path has a list of problems. What if the upload fails? What if the file is corrupted? And the API servers must be told to reload their index'.

answer: A parallel setup: upload the new dictionary to a new, versioned path (s3://word-dictionary/dictionary1.dictionary serving, dictionary2.dictionary this week's) while the old keeps serving. Open question: how do you tell the API servers this is the new path to serve?
evidence: Ch6 §6.2: 'That leaves one open question: how do you tell the API servers that this is the new path they should start serving?'

answer: It kills portability - the dictionary must stay one file (the lookup would build a path like /z/zoo.txt).
evidence: Ch6 §6.2: 'One file per word... That kills portability, the very constraint this design is playing with'.

answer: A small metadata file (meta.json) on S3 holds the path of the current dictionary. The job uploads the new file and only in the PUT's success callback updates the metadata; API servers poll it every 5-10 minutes and, when the path changes, fetch the new file and rebuild their in-memory index. The meta file's own path must be static, never versioned, so everyone knows the one place to look.
evidence: Ch6 §6.2: 'the metadata file's own path is static, never versioned, so everyone knows it is the only place to look.'

evidence: Ch6 §6.3: 'the exact upload time isn't known... S3 might be down, and the upload only lands on Monday... That isn't a reason to poll.'

answer: Reactive: every API server subscribes to a Redis Pub/Sub channel; when the update server finishes uploading it publishes an event and every server receives it. answer: Latest flag (0/1 in each header, old set to 0): a server would never know which file is latest unless it polled. Checking the version on each request: you can't know something changed unless you poll, so it's still polling.
evidence: Ch6 §6.3: 'how would a server know which file is the latest? It never would, unless it polled'; 'this is still polling.'

answer: No. Polling isn't bad; it's just that with one update a week, why make 5,000 requests to find out when someone can tell you or trigger something instead.
evidence: Ch6 §6.3: 'Polling isn't bad, and this isn't an argument against it. It's just that with one update a week, why make 5,000 requests'.

answer: Old orders (6+ months) are rarely opened, so push them to S3 while recent ones stay in the hot DB (MySQL). evidence: Ch6 §6.5: 'push orders older than six months to S3... you need the ability to make pointed queries on S3, order ID in, order details out'.

evidence: Ch6 §6.5: 'Keeping very infrequently accessed data on S3 trades time for money... The latency is acceptable because the reads are infrequent.'

answer: The page doesn't say what was promised for after the break; it only describes the second problem as a super fast KV store on commodity magnetic disks - 'a database most people use without knowing it', with O(1) reads/writes/deletes plus persistence, going deeper into the file format to get the maximum out of the disk.

answer: Support put, get, update and delete, super fast, with full persistence (every put flushed to disk immediately), on very commodity hardware: cheap magnetic hard disks.
evidence: Ch7 §7.1: 'Design a super fast key-value store on very commodity hardware: cheap magnetic hard disks. It must support put, get, update and delete, with full persistence.'

answer: SSDs sit closer to memory than magnetic HDDs in both speed and cost (memory -> SSD -> HDD: faster/costlier to slower/cheaper). SSDs are very costly vs magnetic disks, so huge amounts of data are stored on magnetic disks.
evidence: Ch7 §7.1: 'SSDs sit closer to memory than magnetic hard disks do, both in speed and in cost... huge amounts of data are stored on magnetic disks, not on SSDs.'

answer: A byte offset is translated to a disk, a sector, and an offset in the sector; the disk rotates and the magnetic head physically moves to that location, reads it, sends it to the device driver, then up to user space; each read elsewhere needs another movement. The mechanical movement (moving the head, rotating the disk) is the most time-consuming part.
evidence: Ch7 §7.1: 'That mechanical movement, moving the head and rotating the disk, is the most time-consuming part of disk I/O.'

answer: That every put must be persisted/flushed to disk immediately - a memtable/SSTable holding writes in a sorted in-memory map first doesn't fit that requirement.
evidence: Ch7 §7.2: 'That doesn't fit the requirement as set: every put must be persisted to disk immediately.'

answer: Append every put to the end of one file (a write-ahead-style log/ledger), flushed immediately (open in append mode, write, fsync, then ack). Best on a magnetic disk because the head is already where the last write ended: no seek, no waiting for rotation, no big mechanical movement.
evidence: Ch7 §7.2: 'Append only, zero seek, no big mechanical movement: the best you can do.'

answer: K1 V1' is appended at the end like any other entry (after K3 V3); the old K1 V1 entry isn't touched and simply becomes obsolete.
evidence: Ch7 §7.2: 'The new entry is appended like any other, and the old one simply becomes obsolete.'

answer: Because it's an append-only file: you cannot write to any location other than the end (setting K2's old value to -1 in place isn't allowed).
evidence: Ch7 §7.3: 'But this is an append-only file: you cannot write to any other location.'

answer: Delete is a put with a special marker value appended at the end: DEL K2 = PUT(K2, -1) (and K2 is removed from the in-memory map). That gives an O(1) delete, as efficient as put; dead entries are cleaned up later in the merge.
evidence: Ch7 §7.3: 'Delete is a put with a special value, DEL K2 = PUT(K2, −1).' 'Appends are O(1), so delete is O(1) too.'

answer: Naive: scan from the top, look at every entry, return the latest for the key - very poor. Made fast with an in-memory hash table mapping each key to the offset (not the value) of its latest entry; a get goes straight to that offset: one memory lookup, one disk read.
evidence: Ch7 §7.4: 'Keep an in-memory hash table that maps each key to the offset of its latest entry in the file'.

answer: Allows random reads anywhere in what was written; forbids random writes - writes only at the end.
evidence: Ch7 §7.3: 'Random reads, yes; random writes, no.'

answer: Each put first appends to the file, then the map is updated: K1->O1, K2->O2, K3->O3. PUT K1 V1' is appended at O4, then K1 is repointed to O4 (old K1 V1 obsolete). DEL K2 appends 'K2 -1' at O5 and removes K2 from the map. Final map: K1->O4, K3->O3, no K2.
evidence: Ch7 §7.4 Clip 7·1 text and Fig 7·b complete: 'K1 → O4 · K3 → O3 · no K2: deleted'.

answer: GET: look up the key in the map; no entry -> 404 (no disk read); entry -> read once at that offset and return the value. After a crash the map is gone but the file is safe; on restart read the whole file from the top and rebuild the map (later entries win, -1 removes the key) - slow, accepted for this design.
evidence: Ch7 §7.4: 'If the machine dies, the hash table is gone. The file is safe on disk, though, so on restart you go through the entire file and rebuild the index. That can take a long time'.

answer: Every key must fit in memory (values stay on disk), so you can store only as many keys as fit in RAM; also restarts are slow since the map must be rebuilt by scanning.
evidence: Ch8 §8.1: 'every key has to fit in memory... So you can store only as many keys as you can keep in RAM.'

answer: The store only appends and never collects, so the file grows huge and the system eventually runs out of disk space. Against one/huge files: while scanning one huge file you can't build the in-memory index concurrently; cleaning smaller pieces is more even; and the biggest reason: the file system may not support files beyond about a terabyte (BTRFS, NTFS have limits). (Page caveat: modern file systems allow many TB; the stronger reason is that merge, compaction and rebuilds work file by file.)
evidence: Ch8 §8.1 and §8.2: 'The biggest reason of all is the file system. It is quite possible that your file system does not support files of more than a terabyte'.

answer: Keep smaller files, say 100 MB or 1 GB, with file rotation: as soon as the active file crosses the threshold, start a new one (real Bitcask: 2 GB default).
evidence: Ch8 §8.2: 'keep smaller files: say 100 MB, or 1 GB. As soon as the active file crosses that threshold, start writing to a new one.'

answer: Exactly one active file takes all writes; all other files are read-only (immutable) but can still be read - a get goes to whichever file holds the key, active or older. The map must now store the file and the offset per key (e.g. K1 -> f1, O4).
evidence: Ch8 §8.2: 'exactly one file is active, and all writes go to it. Every other file is read-only, but it can still be read'; 'K1 → f1, O4'.

answer: A separate process, while the active file keeps taking writes, iterates the read-only files and writes one new combined file without stale or deleted entries; then the old files are deleted forever. Afterwards the in-memory map must be updated (atomically, per the prepared notes) for every entry that moved to the new file/offsets.
evidence: Ch8 §8.3: 'the in-memory map must be updated for every entry that moved into the new file. The prepared notes add one word: update it atomically.'

answer: A sawtooth: usage climbs with writes and drops suddenly at each merge and compaction. It is bounded by the disk's maximum capacity (e.g. a 1 TB cap); crossing it crashes the system.
evidence: Ch8 §8.4: 'You will see this sawtooth pattern'; 'If the disk is 1 TB, you cannot let usage grow beyond 1 TB.'

answer: Merge & compaction frequency, and the file rotation threshold (how big a file may grow). Tune them by monitoring the sawtooth while building the store, then decide; expose both as configurable parameters. Merge too often: too much garbage collection, the CPU isn't free for real work. Too rarely: work piles up and a peak can hit the disk cap and crash the store.
evidence: Ch8 §8.4: 'So this design has two configurable parameters... How do you set them? By looking at the sawtooth.' 'Merge too often... Merge too rarely'.

answer: You still get benefits but not as significant: SSDs use flash, not a rotating disk, and handle writes well on their own. (Page adds: flash can't be overwritten in place, so append-only stays flash-friendly; zoned SSDs require sequential writes.)
evidence: Ch8 §8.4: 'On SSDs you still get benefits, but not as significant, because SSDs don't use a rotating disk; they use flash memory'.

answer: Files are read in blocks, not lines; reading one byte at a time until the newline means one disk I/O (read call) per byte, very slow ('code a school kid would write'). (Page caveat: the page cache means most calls don't reach the disk, but it is still slow.)
evidence: Ch9 §9.1: 'if you read one byte at a time until you hit \n, you make one disk I/O per byte, and that makes things very slow.'

answer: Prefix each record with key size and value size, 4-byte integers each (8 bytes together). A read is two disk I/Os: first read the 8 bytes (KSZ, VSZ), add them, then the second I/O reads exactly KSZ+VSZ bytes, split into key and value - read predictability, the same idea as the dictionary header.
evidence: Ch9 §9.1: 'Each is a 4-byte integer, 8 bytes together'; 'Reading a record is now two disk I/Os.'

answer: A crash halfway through writing a gigantic value (e.g. '110' written, then power lost) leaves a corrupt/partial entry; you can't fix it but must know it lost integrity and not serve it. It is dangerous also because after restart the next entry is appended right after the broken one, so reading 'value size' bytes runs into the next entry and returns garbage.
evidence: Ch9 §9.2: 'If you then read value size bytes from the broken entry, the read runs into the entry after it.'

answer: CRC = cyclic redundancy check, a checksum (simple hash) over everything in the record: key size, value size, key and value; compute it on the record built in memory and store it with the record. Placed leftmost because it's the first thing written and flushed - the bare minimum needed to know something is corrupted (can't be at the end); same instinct as distributed ID generators putting the timestamp leftmost. Examples cited: the Postgres commit log and MySQL binlog put the CRC leftmost; network formats too. (Page correction: Bitcask and LevelDB put it first; Postgres WAL and MySQL binlog place it elsewhere - a convention, not a rule.)
evidence: Ch9 §9.2: 'Good persistent record formats do this: the Postgres commit log puts the CRC on the leftmost side, and so does the MySQL binlog' and the 'More precisely' note.

answer: CRC | TS (timestamp) | KSZ | VSZ | K | V. The timestamp is just for conflicts (real Bitcask uses this exact order).
evidence: Ch9 §9.2: 'So the final record is: CRC, timestamp (just for conflicts), key size, value size, key, value.'

answer: Writes are in order: header part, then the key in one write, then the possibly gigantic value in another. If the first write fails, the entry doesn't exist. If a later write fails, on read the CRC doesn't match -> tell the user the entry is corrupted; never serve it. Recovery is heuristic: ignore that entry in merge/compaction and elsewhere and assume the write never came.
evidence: Ch9 §9.2: 'If the first write itself fails, the entry doesn't exist... on read you check the CRC... You ignore that entry, in merge and compaction and elsewhere'.

answer: Per the prepared slides: for each key, file id, entry (value) size, offset (value position) and timestamp. A GET: 1) hash table lookup, 2) disk seek, 3) disk read.
evidence: Ch10 §10.1 Fig 10·a: 'file id · vsz · vpos · ts'; 'GET(k) → ... 1 · hash table lookup · 2 · disk seek · 3 · disk read'; 'Redrawn from the three prepared slides'.

answer: Bitcask's entries are not sorted (they are in write order), so a merge-sort two-pointer merge doesn't work; instead load the entries into a temporary hash table (newer entries replace a key, deletes remove it), then flush. The dictionary's files were both sorted, so a two-pointer merge worked.
evidence: Ch8 §8.3: 'It is not like the merge step of merge sort, because these entries are not sorted... here the files are in write order, so a hash table does the work.'

answer: Limitation: all keys must fit in memory (the number of keys you can fit decides capacity). Strengths: O(1) put/delete/get; very high write throughput and very low write latency; a read is one memory lookup + one random read; I/O saturation of the device and network (good - getting the most out of the hardware); easy backups (just copy the files).
evidence: Ch10 §10.1: 'All the keys must fit in memory'; 'very high write throughput and very low write latency'; 'I/O saturation'; 'backups are easy'.

answer: Bitcask - an embedded database (like a library inside your program, no separate server, like SQLite); a key-value store.
evidence: Ch10 §10.2: 'The database we just designed is called Bitcask. It is an embedded database.'

answer: As taught: in an SSTable design you also keep values in memory, while Bitcask doesn't; SSTables are also sorted (covered next week). Second: persistence - Bitcask writes every write to disk immediately by default, while a memtable buffers writes and writes them later, so data can be lost if memory goes down. evidence: Ch10 §10.3: 'The big difference, as taught: in an SSTable design you also keep values in memory, while Bitcask does not'; 'The second difference is persistence'.

answer: Nothing special: open the file in append mode ('a', among r, w, r+, w+, a) and start writing; you don't preallocate e.g. a contiguous 1 GB and track usage. Laying out the file on disk is the file system's job (BTRFS, NTFS, ext2/3/4), which marks a large chunk for a file and spaces files out, so growth isn't a problem.
evidence: Ch7 §7.2: 'You don't reserve space up front, say a contiguous 1 GB... you open the file and start writing.'

answer: No special case: when read-only files are merged, stale and deleted entries are simply skipped (a delete removes the key from the temporary hash table), so they are never copied to disk again.
evidence: Ch8 §8.3: 'Deleted keys need no special case... the stale entries and the deleted entries are simply skipped'.

answer: The class answer: yes, writing the header is atomic; the pattern assumes a header smaller than the block size is written whole by the kernel, but kernels/file systems give different guarantees, so behaviour can differ across kernels. The header is tiny (~20 bytes), so in practice it will be written. More paranoid systems keep a separate WAL (left open; the pattern here is more performant). Page note: POSIX/disks don't promise it, but a torn header fails the CRC anyway; Postgres uses full_page_writes.
evidence: Ch9 §9.3: 'The answer given in class was yes: writing the header is atomic'; 'roughly 20 bytes. In practice it will be written'; 'More paranoid systems... keep a separate WAL'.
